processing: Accounts differ: withering or spreading, fixing, rolling and drying as for a green tea, in some descriptions with a degree of oxidation that puts it between green and black. Made both in strips and in small snail shapes.
harvest_season: Little is recorded about picking dates for this tea; as with other Guangxi mountain teas, spring is the season to look for.
appearance_dry: Firm, stout, even strips, or plump snail-shaped pieces that show down; darker lots are glossy and almost black.
appearance_liquor: Clear and bright; shade varies with how the lot was processed, from green-yellow to deeper gold.
appearance_wet: Thick, whole leaf, brighter in greener lots.
taste_profile: Full and fresh with a touch of sweetness and a fruity aroma, and it keeps giving over several steeps.

brewing.notes: Start at 85°C for a green lot; if yours is dark and more oxidised, go hotter. Sturdy leaf, so it takes re-steeping.

vintage_note: Usually sold like other regional Chinese greens, as the latest season's crop and best drunk within a year. Since the name covers different styles, check the colour and ask how it was made; no fixed vintage system is known for it.
description:
Longji tea grows in Longsheng County north of Guilin, around the famous Longji rice terraces, with gardens above 800 metres. It is a regional name more than a tightly defined style, which is the first thing to know before buying.

Filed here as a green tea, it does not always behave like one. Some descriptions list spreading, rolling and a controlled oxidation that sits between green and black, while others describe glossy dark, downy snail shapes. So two bags with this name may look quite different.

The common thread is a stout, long-lasting leaf with a fruity aroma, a full fresh body and some sweetness. Brew by colour: cooler for green lots, hotter for dark ones. Taste the first cup and adjust.

Look for the place on the label, and ask the seller how the tea was processed. The cool, misty, wet climate is a good sign for character, but the terraces' fame is also a selling point, so judge by the leaf.
history:
The main historical claim is that Longji tea was sent as tribute in the Qianlong era, supported by a stone tablet in Pingduan village. It is listed in Chinese tea reference works, although little else is documented about its early story.

The modern industry is clearer. By 2014 Longsheng County reported about 2,000 hectares and 3,000 tonnes a year, with thirteen processing factories, two nurseries and two cooperatives.
